```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(readr)
  library(sf)
  library(terra)
  library(knitr)
})

out_dir <- "output/unified"

read_data <- function(filename) {
  read_csv(
    file.path(out_dir, filename),
    show_col_types = FALSE
  )
}

journeys <- read_data(
  "Table_assigned_travel_times.csv"
)

routes <- read_data(
  "walking_route_distances.csv"
)

coverage <- read_data(
  "Table_spatial_accessibility_summary.csv"
)

validation <- read_data(
  "Table_accessibility_validation.csv"
)

ss51 <- read_csv(
  "output/network_51/ss_51.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(journeys) == 176,
  nrow(routes) == 88,
  nrow(validation) == 10,
  all(validation$missing_values == 0),
  all(validation$origins == validation$zero_hour_origins)
)

clean_site <- function(x) {
  z <- iconv(
    trimws(as.character(x)),
    to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT"
  )
  z[is.na(z)] <- x[is.na(z)]
  gsub("[^a-z0-9]", "", tolower(z))
}

walking <- journeys |>
  filter(mode == "walking") |>
  transmute(
    network,
    province,
    sentinel_site,
    site_key = clean_site(sentinel_site),
    dps_office,
    dps_longitude,
    dps_latitude,
    site_longitude,
    site_latitude,
    straight_km,
    walk_h = travel_hours
  )

motorized <- journeys |>
  filter(mode == "motorized") |>
  transmute(
    network,
    province,
    site_key = clean_site(sentinel_site),
    motor_h = travel_hours
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(walking) == 88,
  nrow(motorized) == 88
)

join_keys <- c(
  "network", "province", "site_key"
)

stopifnot(
  !anyDuplicated(walking[join_keys]),
  !anyDuplicated(motorized[join_keys])
)

pairs <- walking |>
  inner_join(
    motorized,
    by = join_keys
  )

route_data <- routes |>
  mutate(
    site_key = clean_site(sentinel_site)
  ) |>
  select(
    network,
    province,
    site_key,
    walking_route_km
  )

stopifnot(
  !anyDuplicated(route_data[join_keys])
)

pairs <- pairs |>
  left_join(
    route_data,
    by = join_keys
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(pairs) == 88,
  !anyNA(pairs$walking_route_km)
)

net11 <- pairs |>
  filter(network == 11)

net26 <- pairs |>
  filter(network == 26)

net51 <- pairs |>
  filter(network == 51)

stopifnot(
  nrow(net11) == 11,
  nrow(net26) == 26,
  nrow(net51) == 51
)

# Identify the 15 additions in 2014

historical_keys <- unique(net11$site_key)

historical_current <- net26 |>
  filter(site_key %in% historical_keys)

additions2014 <- net26 |>
  filter(!site_key %in% historical_keys)

stopifnot(
  nrow(historical_current) == 11,
  nrow(additions2014) == 15
)

# Identify the 25 proposed additions in 2021

proposed_keys <- ss51 |>
  filter(network == "2021_expansion") |>
  pull(sentinel_site) |>
  clean_site()

stopifnot(
  length(proposed_keys) == 25,
  !anyDuplicated(proposed_keys)
)

additions2021 <- net51 |>
  filter(site_key %in% proposed_keys)

stopifnot(nrow(additions2021) == 25)

# Match historical sites under old and modern DPS assignments

reassignment <- net11 |>
  select(
    site_key,
    site = sentinel_site,
    historical_province = province,
    old_dps = dps_office,
    old_lon = dps_longitude,
    old_lat = dps_latitude,
    old_walk_h = walk_h,
    old_motor_h = motor_h
  ) |>
  inner_join(
    historical_current |>
      select(
        site_key,
        current_province = province,
        current_dps = dps_office,
        new_lon = dps_longitude,
        new_lat = dps_latitude,
        new_walk_h = walk_h,
        new_motor_h = motor_h
      ),
    by = "site_key"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    different_dps_location =
      abs(old_lon - new_lon) > 1e-6 |
      abs(old_lat - new_lat) > 1e-6,

    walk_difference_h = new_walk_h - old_walk_h,

    direction = case_when(
      walk_difference_h < -0.05 ~ "Shorter",
      walk_difference_h > 0.05 ~ "Longer",
      TRUE ~ "Unchanged"
    )
  )

stopifnot(nrow(reassignment) == 11)

# Numerical formatting

f1 <- function(x) {
  sprintf("%.1f", as.numeric(x))
}

f2 <- function(x) {
  sprintf("%.2f", as.numeric(x))
}

med_iqr <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(
    x,
    c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75),
    na.rm = TRUE
  )

  sprintf(
    "%.1f (%.1f–%.1f)",
    q[2], q[1], q[3]
  )
}

n_pct <- function(condition) {
  sprintf(
    "%d (%.0f%%)",
    sum(condition, na.rm = TRUE),
    100 * mean(condition, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

coverage_pct <- function(network_id, mode_id, hours) {

  x <- coverage |>
    filter(
      network == network_id,
      mode == mode_id,
      threshold_hours == hours
    ) |>
    pull(percent_modelled_area)

  stopifnot(
    length(x) == 1,
    is.finite(x)
  )

  as.numeric(x)
}

# Define unique geographical DPS-to-site journeys

pairs <- pairs |>
  mutate(
    route_key = sprintf(
      "%.8f|%.8f|%.8f|%.8f",
      dps_longitude,
      dps_latitude,
      site_longitude,
      site_latitude
    )
  )

unique_pairs <- pairs |>
  arrange(desc(network)) |>
  distinct(route_key, .keep_all = TRUE)

stopifnot(nrow(unique_pairs) == 52)

# Incremental geographical coverage per added site

gain <- tibble(
  Stage = c("2014 additions", "2021 additions"),
  Added = c(15, 25),

  Walking = c(
    (
      coverage_pct(26, "walking", 24) -
      coverage_pct(11, "walking", 24)
    ) / 15,

    (
      coverage_pct(51, "walking", 24) -
      coverage_pct(26, "walking", 24)
    ) / 25
  ),

  Motorized = c(
    (
      coverage_pct(26, "motorized", 6) -
      coverage_pct(11, "motorized", 6)
    ) / 15,

    (
      coverage_pct(51, "motorized", 6) -
      coverage_pct(26, "motorized", 6)
    ) / 25
  )
)
```

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

**Background:** Malaria transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is characterized by considerable geographical and ecological heterogeneity, with variation in malaria vector species composition, abundance and insecticide resistance across different settings. Entomological sentinel surveillance is essential for monitoring these variations and informing vector control interventions.However, the selection and geographical distribution of sentinel sites can influence both the representativeness of surveillance data and the feasibility of routine monitoring. In the DRC, the national sentinel network expanded from 11 sites in 2003–2005 to 26 in 2014, with 25 additional sites identified for a proposed expansion in 2021. Despite these developments, how network expansion has affected gepgraphical coverage and the travel requirements associated with routine surveillance remains insufficiently understood.

**Methods:** We reconstructed and geocoded the historical 11-site network, the established 26-site network and the proposed configuration of 51 identified sites. Using the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) 2020 walking-only and motorised friction surfaces, we estimated least-cost travel times from each DPS office to its assigned sentinel sites, as well as national accessibility to the nearest DPS office and sentinel site. We also estimated least-cost walking-route distances. All configurations were evaluated using the same friction surfaces.

**Results:** Median assigned walking time was `r f1(median(net11$walk_h))` hours in the historical network, `r f1(median(net26$walk_h))` hours in the established network and `r f1(median(net51$walk_h))` hours in the proposed configuration. The corresponding motorised times were `r f1(median(net11$motor_h))`, `r f1(median(net26$motor_h))` and `r f1(median(net51$motor_h))` hours. The 25 proposed sites were relatively remote, with a median walking time of `r f1(median(additions2021$walk_h))` hours and a median motorised time of `r f1(median(additions2021$motor_h))` hours; `r sum(additions2021$walk_h > 24)` required more than 24 hours of modelled walking travel. The proportion of modelled national area within 24 walking hours of a sentinel site increased from `r f1(coverage_pct(11, "walking", 24))`% to `r f1(coverage_pct(26, "walking", 24))`% and `r f1(coverage_pct(51, "walking", 24))`%. Within six motorised hours, coverage increased from `r f1(coverage_pct(11, "motorized", 6))`% to `r f1(coverage_pct(26, "motorized", 6))`% and `r f1(coverage_pct(51, "motorized", 6))`%.

**Conclusions:** Network expansion improved geographical access to sentinel sites but increased travel requirements for some DPS-to-site journeys. Geographic coverage and operational accessibility are distinct dimensions of surveillance-network performance. Future site selection should consider both alongside ecological representativeness, surveillance frequency and operational capacity.

*Keywords:* malaria; entomological surveillance; sentinel sites; geographic accessibility; friction surfaces; Democratic Republic of the Congo.

# Introduction

Malaria remains a major public health challenge in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which accounted for an estimated 12.5% of global malaria cases and 11.1% of malaria deaths in 2024 [@who2025world]. Vector-control interventions depend on entomological surveillance to monitor vector species, abundance, behaviour and insecticide resistance, and to provide evidence for planning and evaluating interventions [@kouassi2023entomological].

## Background and problem definition

The National Malaria Control Programme (NMCP) monitors malaria vectors through a network of entomological sentinel sites coordinated by Provincial Health Divisions (*Divisions Provinciales de la Santé*, DPS). The network initially comprised 11 sites established during 2003–2005, corresponding to the former 11 provinces. Fifteen additional sites were introduced in 2014, increasing the network to 26. A further expansion was proposed in 2021, with 25 additional sites identified in the available dataset. The present study therefore analyses 51 sites, rather than the complete 52-site configuration envisaged in the planning records.

The historical selection of sentinel sites has been strongly influenced by administrative criteria. Metelo et al. [@metelo2024complexity] highlighted the need to incorporate ecological considerations into sentinel-site selection to improve the representation of vector diversity and epidemiological conditions.

Geographical accessibility is another important consideration because entomological surveillance requires repeated field collections, supervision and transportation of personnel, equipment and biological specimens. Sites that are more difficult to reach may require greater resources to sustain routine surveillance activities.

However, accessibility alone does not establish whether a surveillance location adequately represents the ecological conditions or vector populations of the country. Locations selected primarily because they are easy to reach may fail to capture environmental heterogeneity, while remote locations selected to improve spatial representation may be more difficult to monitor regularly.

This study addresses the geographical and operational dimensions of surveillance-network expansion. Specifically, it examines how changes in the number and location of sentinel sites have affected geographical access and the modelled travel required between DPS offices and their assigned sites.

## Literature review

Entomological surveillance provides evidence on vector abundance, species composition, biting behaviour and insecticide resistance. Such information supports vector-control decisions when sampling is sufficiently standardised and maintained over time [@kouassi2023entomological].

In the DRC, sentinel-site data have been used to investigate insecticide resistance and associated mechanisms [@watsenga2020intensity; @pelloquin2025novel]. Nevertheless, the distribution of surveillance locations influences which vector populations and environmental conditions are represented. Metelo et al. [@metelo2024complexity] identified limitations associated with administrative site selection and emphasised the relevance of ecological characteristics to surveillance design.

Spatial sampling methods offer opportunities to improve geographical and ecological representativeness. Sedda et al. [@sedda2019improved] proposed an ecological stratification approach using standardised environmental information, while Longbottom et al. [@longbottom2020quantifying] combined geographical accessibility and vector-related information to support the selection of monitoring locations.

Travel time can also influence the frequency with which surveillance activities can be conducted. The TIMESS framework developed by Sedda et al. [@sedda2024timess] considers the number of sampling locations and repeated observations while accounting for seasonality and clustering. This highlights the importance of considering both spatial distribution and temporal sampling effort when designing surveillance networks.

Geographical accessibility can be estimated using friction surfaces that represent variation in travel speed across landscapes [@weiss2018global; @weiss2020global]. Such approaches have been applied to examine access to health services in the DRC [@mbunga2024zero; @pu2020improving], but their application to the operational accessibility of malaria entomological sentinel sites remains limited.

The present study contributes to this evidence by comparing historical and proposed sentinel-site configurations using a consistent travel-time modelling framework.

## Research aim and objectives

The aim was to assess changes in the geographical distribution and accessibility of entomological sentinel sites across historical and proposed network configurations in the DRC.

The objectives were:

1. To map and compare the distribution of sentinel sites in the historical 11-site, established 26-site and proposed 51-site configurations.
2. To estimate walking and motorised travel times between DPS offices and their assigned sentinel sites.
3. To assess national accessibility to the nearest DPS office and the nearest sentinel site.
4. To estimate modelled walking-route distances and examine their implications for surveillance operations.

# Methods

## Study area and network configurations

The analysis covered the DRC, a country of approximately 2.3 million km² characterised by extensive forests, savannas, wetlands, rivers and considerable variation in transport infrastructure.

The historical 2003–2005 configuration comprised 11 sentinel sites associated with the former 11 provinces. The 2014 configuration included 26 sites, while the proposed 2021 configuration comprised the 26 established sites and 25 additional identified locations.

The historical network was mapped using the former 11 provincial boundaries. The established and proposed configurations were mapped using current provincial boundaries derived from GRID3 DRC health-zone data v9.0 [@ciesin2026grid3].

The same MAP 2020 friction surfaces were used across all configurations. The analyses therefore compare alternative network arrangements under fixed modelled transport conditions rather than reconstructing historical changes in road infrastructure.

## Data sources and geocoding

The analysis combined sentinel-site records compiled from NMCP documentation, DPS locations, historical and contemporary administrative boundaries, and walking-only and motorised friction surfaces.

The coordinates of sentinel sites and DPS locations were compiled through a geocoding workflow that included Google Maps, GRID3, Nominatim and Photon. Administrative and geographical consistency checks were used to identify potential errors in site locations and assignments.

The Katana location in Sud-Kivu was corrected following review of an initial geocoding error. Historical and current administrative names were retained as appropriate, including sites such as Mikalayi, which appears under different provincial names across network configurations.

DPS locations were represented by the available coordinates of their administrative seats rather than independently verified office entrances. Some sentinel-site coordinates similarly represent settlements rather than exact collection locations.

## Least-cost travel-time modelling

Travel times were estimated from the MAP 2020 walking-only and motorised friction surfaces [@weiss2020global], accessed through `malariaAtlas` [@pfeffer2018malariaatlas].

The friction surfaces have an approximate spatial resolution of 1 km and represent movement costs in minutes per metre. They were prepared for the DRC with a 50-km surrounding buffer to accommodate routes near national boundaries.

For each transport mode, the raster surface was converted into a transition graph with eight-neighbour connectivity. Conductance between neighbouring cells was defined as the inverse of the mean friction value and corrected for geographical distance using `gdistance::geoCorrection(type = "c")` [@vanetten2017gdistance].

The friction surfaces' existing treatment of water was retained where valid values were available. Cells without valid movement costs were not assigned traversable connections. The analysis did not explicitly model ferry waiting times, boat schedules, road closures or seasonal changes in accessibility.

Assigned travel times between DPS offices and sentinel sites were calculated using `gdistance::costDistance()`. Separate origin–destination matrices were generated for the 11-, 26- and 51-site configurations under walking and motorised transport.

National accessibility to the nearest DPS office and to the nearest sentinel site was calculated using `gdistance::accCost()`.

The historical nearest-DPS analysis used 11 offices, while the established and proposed configurations used the same 26 offices. In contrast, the nearest-sentinel analysis used 11, 26 and 51 site locations, respectively.

Travel-time thresholds were selected to describe different planning horizons. For assigned journeys, walking times exceeding 24 hours were used to identify particularly prolonged continuous walking requirements, while motorised journeys of at least two hours were considered relevant to planning same-day round trips. These thresholds are descriptive rather than verified operational limits.

For national geographical coverage, walking thresholds of 6, 12, 24, 48 and 72 hours and motorised thresholds of 1, 3, 6, 12 and 24 hours were used to describe changes across short and long travel horizons.

Geographical coverage was calculated as the percentage of modelled national area accessible within each threshold, using area-weighted raster cells and a consistent national boundary. These values do not represent population coverage or ecological representativeness.

## Walking-route distances

Least-cost walking routes between DPS offices and assigned sentinel sites were calculated using `gdistance::shortestPath()`.

The resulting spatial lines were used to estimate geodesic route lengths. Identical origin–destination coordinate pairs were identified and treated as repeated geographical journeys where they appeared in more than one network configuration.

The analysis included 88 walking network-scenario journey records corresponding to 52 distinct DPS-to-site coordinate pairs.

Route distances describe the length of the least-cost path across the modelled friction surface and should not be interpreted as observed walking distances.

Motorised route distances were not calculated in the present analysis; motorised results are therefore reported as travel times only.

## Quality assurance and reproducibility

The analytical workflow included checks of site assignments, origin–destination travel times, accessibility rasters and route-distance records. Validated outputs were retained in `output/unified/`. Further details of the quality-control checks and software environment are provided in the Supplementary Material.

# Results

## Evolution of the sentinel-site network

The geographical distribution of sentinel sites expanded from 11 historical locations to 26 established sites and subsequently to 51 identified sites in the proposed configuration (@fig-network).

The proposed network includes 25 additional locations distributed across the current provincial structure, with one further planned site in Kasaï-Central not identified in the available records.

```{r}
#| label: fig-network
#| fig-cap: "Evolution of the DRC entomological sentinel-site network: 11 historical sites (2003–2005), 26 established sites (2014) and 51 identified sites in the proposed expansion (2021)."
#| out-width: "90%"

knitr::include_graphics(
  "output/unified/Figure1_network_evolution_clean.png"
)
```

## Assigned DPS-to-sentinel travel times

The analysis modelled 88 assigned DPS-to-sentinel journeys under each transport mode (@tbl-assigned; @fig-assigned). Because existing sites were retained across network configurations, the results are presented for the complete networks and separately for sites added in 2014 and proposed in 2021.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-assigned
#| tbl-cap: "Modelled DPS-to-assigned-sentinel travel times and distances. Travel times and distances are reported as median (interquartile range). Count columns show n (%)."

configurations <- list(
  "2003–2005: 11 sites" = net11,
  "2014 additions: 15" = additions2014,
  "2014 total: 26" = net26,
  "2021 additions: 25" = additions2021,
  "Proposed total: 51" = net51
)

assigned_table <- bind_rows(
  lapply(
    names(configurations),
    function(label) {

      x <- configurations[[label]]

      tibble(
        Configuration = label,
        Sites = nrow(x),
        `Within 1 km` = n_pct(
          x$straight_km <= 1
        ),
        `Walking (h)` = med_iqr(x$walk_h),
        `Walking >24 h` = n_pct(
          x$walk_h > 24
        ),
        `Motorised (h)` = med_iqr(x$motor_h),
        `Motorised >=2 h` = n_pct(
          x$motor_h >= 2
        ),
        `Route km, median (max)` = sprintf(
          "%.1f (%.1f)",
          median(x$walking_route_km),
          max(x$walking_route_km)
        )
      )
    }
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  assigned_table,
  align = "lccccccc"
)
```

### Historical network and DPS reassignment

Under the historical administrative structure, the 11 original sentinel sites had a median assigned walking time of `r f1(median(net11$walk_h))` hours (IQR `r f1(quantile(net11$walk_h, 0.25))`–`r f1(quantile(net11$walk_h, 0.75))`) and a median motorised time of `r f1(median(net11$motor_h))` hours.

When the same historical sites were examined under the current DPS assignments, `r sum(reassignment$different_dps_location)` were associated with DPS offices at different geographical coordinates. Walking travel times were shorter for `r sum(reassignment$direction == "Shorter")` sites, unchanged for `r sum(reassignment$direction == "Unchanged")` and longer for `r sum(reassignment$direction == "Longer")`. Their median walking time under the current assignment was `r f1(median(reassignment$new_walk_h))` hours.

The comparison of individual historical assignments is presented in @tbl-reassignment.

### Sites added in 2014

The 15 sites introduced in 2014 had a median straight-line distance of `r f1(median(additions2014$straight_km))` km from their assigned DPS offices and a median walking time of `r f1(median(additions2014$walk_h))` hours.

Among these additional sites, `r sum(additions2014$straight_km <= 1)` of 15 were located within 1 km of their DPS coordinates.

For the complete established network of 26 sites, `r sum(net26$straight_km <= 1)` sites were located within 1 km of their assigned DPS coordinates. The median assigned walking time was `r f1(median(net26$walk_h))` hours, compared with `r f1(median(net11$walk_h))` hours in the historical network.

The comparison of the same historical sites under both assignments helps distinguish the effect of administrative reassignment from the effect of adding locations close to DPS offices.

Locations within 1 km should be interpreted as geographically proximate; this does not demonstrate that their surveillance facilities and DPS offices occupy the same building.

### Sites proposed in 2021

The 25 proposed additional sites had a median straight-line distance of `r f1(median(additions2021$straight_km))` km (IQR `r f1(quantile(additions2021$straight_km, 0.25))`–`r f1(quantile(additions2021$straight_km, 0.75))`) from their assigned DPS offices.

Their median walking time was `r f1(median(additions2021$walk_h))` hours (IQR `r f1(quantile(additions2021$walk_h, 0.25))`–`r f1(quantile(additions2021$walk_h, 0.75))`), and their median motorised time was `r f1(median(additions2021$motor_h))` hours.

Among the 25 proposed sites, `r n_pct(additions2021$walk_h > 24)` required more than 24 hours of modelled walking travel, while `r n_pct(additions2021$motor_h >= 2)` required at least two hours of modelled motorised travel.

Including the proposed sites increased the median assigned walking time of the complete 51-site configuration to `r f1(median(net51$walk_h))` hours and the median motorised time to `r f1(median(net51$motor_h))` hours. The maximum assigned journeys reached `r f1(max(net51$walk_h))` hours on foot and `r f1(max(net51$motor_h))` hours under motorised travel.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of modelled walking and motorised DPS-to-assigned-sentinel travel times across historical, established and proposed network configurations."
#| out-width: "95%"

knitr::include_graphics(
  "output/unified/Figure4_assigned_travel_time_distributions.png"
)
```

## National geographical accessibility to sentinel sites

The national accessibility analysis showed that increasing the number of sentinel sites reduced modelled travel time to the nearest surveillance location across substantial areas of the country (@fig-sentinel).

::: {#fig-sentinel layout-ncol="1"}

![Walking-only accessibility across the 11-, 26- and 51-site configurations.](output/unified/FigureS1_walking_nearest_sentinel_sites.png){width=100%}

![Motorised accessibility across the 11-, 26- and 51-site configurations.](output/unified/FigureS2_motorized_nearest_sentinel_sites.png){width=100%}

Modelled accessibility to the nearest sentinel site across the three network configurations. Upper row: walking-only friction surface. Lower row: motorised friction surface. Each row contains the historical 11-site, established 26-site and proposed 51-site configurations.

:::

Within 24 hours of modelled walking travel, the proportion of modelled national area accessible to a sentinel site increased from `r f1(coverage_pct(11, "walking", 24))`% with 11 sites to `r f1(coverage_pct(26, "walking", 24))`% with 26 sites and `r f1(coverage_pct(51, "walking", 24))`% in the proposed configuration.

Within six hours of motorised travel, the corresponding percentages were `r f1(coverage_pct(11, "motorized", 6))`%, `r f1(coverage_pct(26, "motorized", 6))`% and `r f1(coverage_pct(51, "motorized", 6))`%.

The two selected thresholds are presented in @tbl-coverage, while the full range of thresholds evaluated in the Methods is provided in @tbl-full-coverage.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coverage
#| tbl-cap: "Percentage of modelled DRC area within selected travel-time thresholds of the nearest sentinel site."

coverage_table <- tibble(
  Configuration = c(
    "11 sites",
    "26 sites",
    "51 sites"
  ),
  `Walking <=24 h (%)` = vapply(
    c(11, 26, 51),
    coverage_pct,
    numeric(1),
    mode_id = "walking",
    hours = 24
  ),
  `Motorised <=6 h (%)` = vapply(
    c(11, 26, 51),
    coverage_pct,
    numeric(1),
    mode_id = "motorized",
    hours = 6
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  coverage_table,
  digits = 1,
  align = "lrr"
)
```

### Incremental coverage associated with network expansion

The increase in geographical coverage differed between expansion stages.

For the 24-hour walking threshold, the introduction of 15 sites in 2014 was associated with an average increase of `r f2(gain$Walking[1])` percentage points of national area per additional site. The proposed 2021 additions were associated with an average increase of `r f2(gain$Walking[2])` percentage points per site.

For the six-hour motorised threshold, the corresponding average increases were `r f2(gain$Motorized[1])` and `r f2(gain$Motorized[2])` percentage points per additional site.

These values express the total percentage-point gain associated with each expansion stage divided by the number of sites added. They do not measure the independent contribution of individual sites, nor do they account for potential overlap in their geographical catchments.

## Accessibility to DPS offices

Accessibility to the nearest DPS office also improved when the network of provincial offices increased from 11 historical DPS locations to 26 contemporary DPS locations.

Unlike nearest-sentinel accessibility, the nearest-DPS surfaces did not change between the 2014 and proposed 2021 configurations because both used the same 26 DPS origins.

The walking and motorised nearest-DPS maps, together with the corresponding area-weighted accessibility results, are presented in the Supplementary Material.

# Discussion

## Principal findings

This analysis quantified geographical and operational differences between the historical 11-site, established 26-site and proposed 51-site entomological surveillance networks in the DRC.

Three findings are particularly important.

First, the expansion of the network increased geographical accessibility to sentinel sites, with more of the country falling within selected walking and motorised travel-time thresholds.

Second, the proposed additional sites required longer assigned journeys from their supervising DPS offices than many of the established sites.

Third, the average geographical coverage gained per added site declined between the 2014 and proposed 2021 expansion stages, particularly for motorised travel at the selected six-hour threshold.

The declining average gain may reflect overlapping accessibility areas, saturation at the selected threshold, or differences in the location of newly selected sites. The present descriptive analysis cannot determine the relative contribution of these explanations.

Together, the results demonstrate that expanding geographical coverage and maintaining operational accessibility are related but distinct surveillance-planning objectives.

## Accessibility and ecological representativeness

Although geographical access to sentinel sites improved with network expansion, this does not establish that the expanded network is environmentally or epidemiologically representative.

Sentinel-site selection should consider the ecological conditions represented by surveillance locations, particularly where malaria-vector species differ in habitat requirements or spatial distribution.

Previous work has emphasised the importance of incorporating environmental heterogeneity into vector-surveillance sampling designs [@sedda2019improved; @metelo2024complexity].

Accessibility and ecological conditions may also be associated. Transport infrastructure and settlement patterns are unevenly distributed across landscapes, and locations that are easier to reach may differ from remote areas in vegetation, land cover and other environmental characteristics.

However, the direction and magnitude of this potential bias have not been measured in the present study. Evaluating it would require comparing site locations with national environmental covariates and examining how accessibility relates to those covariates across unsampled areas.

## Operational feasibility and surveillance frequency

Geographical accessibility may influence the resources required to maintain routine entomological surveillance.

For sites requiring prolonged journeys, supervision, collection activities and specimen transport may demand additional staff time and logistical support.

However, travel time alone does not determine the probability of completing planned surveillance visits. Operational feasibility also depends on staffing, funding, transport availability, seasonal conditions, insecurity and laboratory processing capacity.

The TIMESS framework [@sedda2024timess] provides a relevant methodological perspective because surveillance power depends on both the number of locations and the frequency of repeated sampling, particularly where measurements exhibit temporal and spatial correlation.

For the DRC, an operationally feasible surveillance design would therefore need to consider not only where sites should be located but also how regularly those sites can be visited to achieve the intended surveillance objectives.

## Implications for future network design

The present analysis does not determine the optimal number or location of sentinel sites. Rather, it provides an accessibility component that could be incorporated into a broader network-design framework.

Future site selection could consider environmental representativeness, predicted vector suitability, malaria transmission, geographical coverage, operational travel time and programme resources.

Different surveillance objectives may require different sampling designs. Longitudinal insecticide-resistance monitoring, for example, depends on repeat observations at suitable sites, whereas detecting locally restricted vector populations may require wider geographical exploration.

Consequently, an optimal surveillance strategy may involve differentiating the sampling frequency and scientific role of individual sites rather than applying an identical surveillance schedule everywhere.

## Strengths and limitations

A strength of the study is the comparison of three network configurations using consistent friction surfaces, modelling procedures and geographical boundaries.

The analysis distinguishes assigned DPS-to-site travel time, geographical accessibility to DPS offices and geographical accessibility to sentinel sites. These measures describe different aspects of surveillance operations and network coverage.

Nevertheless, the findings are subject to limitations.

The MAP 2020 surfaces were used for all three configurations and therefore do not represent historical transport conditions. The modelled travel times were not validated against observed journeys and do not incorporate waiting times, overnight stays, seasonal flooding, river transport schedules or road closures.

Some coordinates represent settlements or administrative seats rather than exact facility entrances. The approximate 1-km raster resolution also limits interpretation of very short journeys.

The geographical coverage estimates are area-weighted, not population-weighted, and do not measure environmental representativeness or the epidemiological value of sites.

The analysis also did not quantify surveillance costs, sampling-frequency requirements or the likelihood that planned visits would be completed.

Finally, the proposed configuration included 51 identified sites; the additional planned Kasaï-Central site was not available for analysis.

## Future research

Future work should examine how travel time relates to environmental characteristics relevant to malaria vectors across the DRC. This would help determine whether accessible locations systematically differ from poorly accessible areas in their environmental conditions.

Environmental covariates and species-distribution models could then be used to assess how well the existing and proposed networks represent major vector habitats and to identify potentially undersampled ecological regions.

A more comprehensive framework could incorporate operational travel time, sampling frequency, expected survey completion, programme costs and laboratory capacity as constraints on network design.

The resulting analysis could compare alternative site configurations and identify trade-offs between ecological representativeness and operational feasibility, rather than assuming that an increase in site number necessarily improves surveillance efficiency.

# Conclusion

The expansion of the DRC entomological sentinel-site network improved geographical accessibility to surveillance locations, but the proposed additional sites required longer supervisory journeys from their assigned DPS offices.

The results indicate that geographical coverage and operational accessibility represent different dimensions of surveillance-network performance.

Accessibility modelling provides quantitative information to support surveillance planning, but it cannot independently determine whether a network adequately represents vector distributions or national epidemiological heterogeneity.

Future network design should therefore integrate geographical accessibility with ecological representativeness, surveillance objectives, sampling frequency and operational resources.

## Supplementary note: Reproducibility and quality control

Ten accessibility rasters were validated, comprising four nearest-DPS surfaces (two networks × two travel modes) and six nearest-sentinel surfaces (three networks × two travel modes). All source locations returned zero travel time at their corresponding raster origins, and no missing origin values were identified.

The assigned travel-time analysis generated 176 network-scenario records. The walking-route dataset included all 88 walking scenario records and 52 unique coordinate pairs.

The saved walking-route travel times were compared with the current assigned-journey calculations. All 88 records matched, with no missing route distances and a maximum difference of approximately 2.9 minutes, consistent with the precision of previously saved travel times.

The computational workflow comprises the seven numbered scripts `00_packages.R` to `06_run_analysis.R`. The software environment was recorded in `output/unified/R_session_information.txt`, and the model configuration in `output/unified/accessibility_model_configuration.csv`.

A complete reconstruction requires the original coordinate datasets, geographical boundaries, MAP friction surfaces and access to the relevant R packages. The modelling outputs were retained to allow computational checks without repeatedly rebuilding expensive transition matrices.
